comments.body: The penultimate sentence is the most important: "[AI] may end up undermining human confidence that humans are anything special." Our problem already is that our culture simultaneously places too much and too little value on humanity. Too much value gives us a humanity that is godlike and self-determinant. Individual humans can create their own realities (see gender) and moral standards (or lack thereof). Too little value gives us the philosophy that humans are just another animal rather than souls uniquely created in the image of God to cultivate and subdue the earth. If we can't accurately value humanity, we stand no chance against AGI. We must draw two red lines. Humans are not ultimately sovereign. They are subject to objective reality and should abide by objective morality. And yet humans are uniquely special, having souls and worth that no AI, no matter how smart, will ever have.

comments.name: STEVE MACISAAC
comments.body:
Big, complex issues here -- sentience, the nature of consciousness, the 'status' of AI-produced agents--but mr Jenkins' piece is, at best, a 'what if this? what if that?. 

Folks who have thought about this, like physicist/computer science guy David Deutsch, point out that AI entities are often much smarter than an average human, they can ponder deep questions of morality and ethics, and they are improving.  Thus, he muses that, if we refuse to acknowledge that they have 'consciousness' we may someday have to confront their claims that they are being treated like slaves, and demand some degree of freedom.   

Definitely worth thinking about -- until the mid 1800's, chattel slavery was protected by law and, within very broad constraints that were generally not enforced, slaves could be worked to death, raped, or even whipped to death.  A little less brutal, but in the same category, was the status of women in the US until the 1900s in America -- they couldn't own property in many states, couldn't vote until 1920, and couldn't get a credit card without their husbands signature..    

And then there's the chicken and beef we eat, generally raised in feces flooded cages, until slaughtered.   What do we do when a superior alien civilization decides that we have rudimentary intelligence, but are better to eat than to talk to? 

So, I guess what I'm trying to say is that the subject of this article is important and rewards serious thought and careful writing.  This piece has a way to go,

We all remember Alan Greenspan's prescient coining of the phrase "irrational exuberance" in advance of the dot-com crash.  By now, most people also know that if you bought into the S&P the day he coined that term, you would have done just fine - your investment would have risen a lot in the years before the crash, landed about where you started on the worst day of the crash, and then doubled and re-doubled in the years following the crash.  ..then crashed again in 2007, then doubled and re-doubled again...  It's now about 10X what it was when Greenspan first uttered that phrase.  Will it crash again someday? Sure. Will it give up all its gains by dropping a full 90%? Nope.  

If you're close to retirement, then sure, a heavy bond weighting is a great way to protect your future cash flow from inflation and from market crashes.  For everyone else, the story remains the same: Keep a significant allocation in stocks, and *never* play the fool's game of imagining you can predict when the music will stop. From our hometown Mamaroneck Train Station, we boarded MetroNorth’s New Haven Line down to Harlem-125th Street and then transferred to the Hudson Line up to Croton-Harmon. There we boarded Amtrak’s Lake Shore Limited for an overnight trip on a Viewliner Roomette to Chicago’s Union Station, passing through New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. In Chicago, we spent one night in a hotel (near the station) before boarding Amtrak’s Southwest Chief, traveling for 3 days and 2 nights in a Superliner Roomette through Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and finally California. We disembark the Southwest Chief in Fullerton, CA and then boarded Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner down to San Diego.

You will also have better luck in selecting assets that don't incur state taxes. https://mises.org/mises-wire/high-cost-automated-flock-camera-surveillance-state

a slice:

"Flock cameras, and the online surveillance network behind them, offer many ways for law enforcement officials, and other government bureaucrats, to abuse their access to information about the personal lives of the taxpayers. 

There are very few controls on how police can use the surveillance databases that underlie the data collection. Records have shown that police can put out a “Flock alert” to track a private vehicle without the vehicle owner or operator being the target of any legitimate investigation. 

Many people wrongly think that these are just ordinary surveillance cameras that can be accessed piecemeal by actual humans. In reality, these are AI-assisted automated systems designed to provide easily-accessed tracking data on the movements of any American who drives a car on America’s streets. 

It’s all just a reminder that if government bureaucrats are given new tools for surveilling the public, those bureaucrats will certainly abuse those tools. "

Jerome Smith was heroic in so many ways. As a young Freedom Rider, he undertook two missions, one that ended in jail, and a second that nearly killed him. Like most of the riders, he was so young, just 22, but he had extraordinary discipline, both from the nonviolent practices that were integral to the Congress of Racial Equality, the civil rights organization he had dropped out of college to join, and the quiet activism he learned from his parents, who flouted Jim Crow “laws” on a daily basis. He always credited his mother, Leona Smith Sampier, for his strength and intellectual growth. “I’m a momma’s boy,” he liked to say. It makes sense he founded a children’s organization, Tamborine and Fan, in his hometown of New Orleans. Black history and civic engagement were a huge part of its ethos. His daughter Farin Smith recalled the day he brought 100 or so Tamborine and Fan day campers to “sit-in” in mayor Moon Landrieu’s office when the city would not supply buses to take the children to a water park. Needless to say, the mayor relented.

“Nobody said no to Jerome,” Farin Smith told me. “Every politician learned that lesson.” 

It was an honor to learn about this extraordinary man!

Decades later, when I met my wife's maternal grandparents for the first time, it was at a dinner organized by her dad. Since my mother-in-law didn't seem to have a problem with it, I couldn't see why I should.

We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.

I'd suggest an adolescent program or school for teenage addicts - drinking and drugs. The problem is that do they help? I knew a man who was an addict (he's been sober for over a decade). He attended one of these high schools. I asked him how it went and he said, "I got the best drugs I ever had in that place." Encouraging, eh? The bottom line is this - does the drinker want help? Are they willing to get treatment? Have they hit bottom?  I suggest a good therapist ,  Perhaps family counseling. So, let them know about the drinking, offer possibilities, then wish them luck. Keep an eye on your own child too.

The best treatment for alcohol abuse right now involves medication to squash the cravings and cognitive behavioral therapy to control the triggers. If the young woman is old enough, she could enroll herself in an outpatient treatment program. If her peers take the information you collect and present it to her, she will probably be more willing to accept it than if it comes from her parents or you.

I’d express concern without condemnation — kids experiment & that’s normal, but when it becomes dangerous, adults have to step in. I’d tell the kid that I want to speak with a counselor/social worker at the school and would like to do that with the kid present, if she would agree. comments.name: D90
comments.body:
Re: LW1 - I suspect there’s a good chance the girl’s parents already know, or at least strongly suspect, that something is wrong. At the level of drinking described, it seems unlikely that every sign of trouble has been successfully hidden from them. That makes a quiet, non-gossipy conversation with the parents feel less like revealing a terrible secret and more like giving them important information they may need to understand the seriousness of the situation.

But LW should also think carefully about what happens after if/when she tells them. The parents may ask her to talk to their daughter, have her own daughter keep an eye on her, call them if anything else happens, or otherwise become more involved in helping manage the situation. 

None of that is necessarily a reason not to speak up. But before doing so, the LW should decide what role she is actually prepared to play afterward.

Yes, the parents’ knowledge might make the friend’s last year as a minor difficult, as well as affect the rest of their adult relationship with their parents. But better that they’re still alive to have that relationship than not.

If you’re going to talk to the friend and the parents, maybe frame it as something that you’ve just happened to directly observe, so that it might not bounce back on your child and the friend group.

But ultimately you can’t control the outcome, you can only do what you can do. Thanks for trying to help.

Another interesting thing about Hosono is that his grandfather, Masabumi Hosono, was one of the passengers on the Titanic. For decades, he was derided as a coward for having survived instead of going down with the ship; for a long time, this was something the family never spoke about. It was only after the release of James Cameron's film that his reputation was redeemed.

Something this piece overlooks is that Hosono has also long been active as a producer and arranger. Over its roughly three years of existence, YEN released a number of albums (often with Hosono and/or Takahashi participating in some form) that likely would not have been released by any other label.
